arml-2007-team-01.title: Slope of a chord
arml-2007-team-01.body:
Let $A=(a,a^2)$ and $B=(b,b^2)$ with $0<a<b$ integers. The slope is $\dfrac{b^2-a^2}{b-a}=a+b$, so we need $a+b=2007$.

Since $a<b$ we need $a<\tfrac{2007}{2}=1003.5$, so $a=1,2,\dots,1003$ and $b=2007-a$ is determined (and automatically larger than $a$). The pairs are $(1,2006),(2,2005),\dots,(1003,1004)$.

**Answer: 1003**

arml-2007-team-03.title: Similar triangles
arml-2007-team-03.body:
Since $AB\parallel CD$, triangles $AME$ and $CDE$ are similar, and $AM=\tfrac12 DC$, so the ratio is $1:2$. Hence $DE=2\cdot EM=8$ and $AE=\tfrac12 EC=5$.

Let $AM=x$ and $AD=y$, so $DC=2x$. Then $DM=DE+EM=12$ and $AC=AE+EC=15$.

- Right triangle $ADM$: $x^2+y^2=12^2=144$.
- Right triangle $ADC$: $(2x)^2+y^2=15^2=225$.

Subtracting: $3x^2=81$, so $x=3\sqrt3$ and $y^2=144-27=117$, $y=3\sqrt{13}$.

Area $=2x\cdot y=6\sqrt3\cdot3\sqrt{13}=18\sqrt{39}$.

**Answer: $18\sqrt{39}$**

arml-2007-team-04.title: Count by blocks
arml-2007-team-04.body:
There are $9^k$ zero-free numbers with $k$ digits, so up to $999$ there are $9+81+729=819$.

- Numbers $1000$–$1999$: leading digit $1$ and three nonzero digits: $9^3=729$, so $819+729=1548$ up to $1999$.
- Numbers $2000$–$2599$: leading digit $2$, a hundreds digit $1$–$5$ and two nonzero digits: $5\cdot81=405$, so $1548+405=1953$ up to $2599$.

We need $2007-1953=54$ more zero-free numbers after $2599$. These begin $2611,\dots$ and (hundreds digit $6$, tens digit $a$, units digit $b$, with $a,b\neq0$) come in groups of $9$ per tens digit. The $54=6\cdot9$th number is the last one with tens digit $6$: $2669$.

**Answer: 2669**

arml-2007-team-04.title: Base 9 idea
arml-2007-team-04.body:
Remove the digit $0$: the zero-free numbers correspond to base-$9$ numerals using digits $1$–$9$ in place of $0$–$8$, i.e. adding $1$ to each digit. The $n$th such number is the base-9 representation of $n$ with every digit increased by 1, applied "bijectively". Writing $2007=2670_9$ would suggest $2670$, but that overcounts by one (the number $0$), so the answer is $2670-1=2669$.

**Answer: 2669**

arml-2007-team-05.title: Case analysis
arml-2007-team-05.body:
Clearing denominators: $x+2=kx^2-x$, i.e. $kx^2-2x-2=0$, with the restriction $kx\neq1$.

- $k=0$: the equation is $\dfrac{x+2}{-1}=x$, giving the single solution $x=-1$.
- $k\neq0$: the quadratic $kx^2-2x-2=0$ has discriminant $4+8k$. A root is spurious only if $kx=1$; substituting $x=\frac1k$ gives $-\frac1k-2=0$, i.e. $k=-\frac12$. For $k=-\frac12$ the discriminant is $0$ with double root $x=-2$, and then $kx-1=0$: the fraction is $\frac00$, so there is no solution at all. For every other $k\neq0$ the quadratic has $0$ or $2$ valid solutions.

So only $k=0$ gives exactly one solution.

**Answer: 0**

arml-2007-team-06.title: Tangent lengths
arml-2007-team-06.body:
For a right triangle with legs $a,b$ and hypotenuse $c$ the inradius is $r=\dfrac{a+b-c}{2}=12$, so $c=a+b-24$.

Squaring: $a^2+b^2=(a+b-24)^2$ simplifies to $ab-24a-24b+288=0$, i.e. $(a-24)(b-24)=288$.

The two factors have the same sign. Both negative is impossible: each leg exceeds $12$ (it contains the tangent length $12$ from the right-angle vertex), so $-12<a-24<0$ and $-12<b-24<0$, giving a product less than $144<288$. So $a-24,\,b-24>0$ and $c=(a-24)+(b-24)+24$.

To maximize $c$ we maximize the sum of two positive integers with product $288$: $1\cdot288$ gives $a=25$, $b=312$, $c=25+312-24=313$.

Check: $25^2+312^2=97969=313^2$ and $\frac{25+312-313}{2}=12$.

**Answer: 313**

arml-2007-team-07.title: Parity of digit counts
arml-2007-team-07.body:
Let $C(p)$ be the number of digits used for pages $1,\dots,p$ and let each chapter use $D$ digits. The $i$th chapter ends at the page $p_i$ with $C(p_i)=iD$, so every multiple $D,2D,\dots,12D$ must be a value taken by $C$.

Values of $C$: $C(p)=p$ for $p\le9$; $C(p)=9+2(p-9)$ is **odd** for $10\le p\le99$ (so $C$ takes only odd values between $11$ and $189$); and for $p\ge100$, $C(p)=189+3(p-99)$, which is a multiple of $3$.

- No multiple of $D$ may be even and lie in $(9,189]$. If $D$ is even all multiples are even, so $D>180$, making $n$ far larger than needed. If $D$ is odd, $2D$ is even, so $2D\le9$ or $2D>189$. $D=1,3$ fail ($4D$, $6D$, ... would be even in the middle range), so $2D\ge190$, i.e. $D\ge95$.
- Then $2D\ge190$ lies in the three-digit region, so $2D$ must be a multiple of $3$, hence $3\mid D$. The smallest odd multiple of $3$ that is at least $95$ is $D=99$.

For $D=99$: chapter 1 ends where $9+2x=99$, i.e. page $54$; chapter 2 ends where $C=198=189+3\cdot3$, page $102$; then each chapter has $33$ three-digit pages. The last page is $n=102+10\cdot33=432$ (check: $C(432)=1188=12\cdot99$).

**Answer: 432**

arml-2007-team-08.title: Discriminant
arml-2007-team-08.body:
A monic quadratic factors over the integers iff its discriminant is a perfect square: $a^2-40a=b^2$. Completing the square, $(a-20)^2-b^2=400$, so $((a-20)+b)((a-20)-b)=400$.

The two factors have the same parity (their sum is even) and their product is even, so both are even. Write them as $2s,2t$ with $st=100$; then $a-20=s+t$. Taking all (positive and negative) factor pairs $(s,t)$ of $100$, with $a-20=s+t$: the values of $a-20$ come in pairs $\pm(s+t)$, so they sum to $0$ over the $10$ distinct values of $a$.

Hence the sum of the $10$ values of $a$ is $10\cdot20=200$.

**Answer: 200**

arml-2007-team-08.title: Pair up the roots
arml-2007-team-08.body:
If $p$ is an integer root, then $a=-\dfrac{p^2}{p+10}$. Set $r=p+10$: $a=-r-\dfrac{100}{r}+20$. Each divisor $r$ of $100$ (positive or negative, $-10\le r\le10$ to avoid duplicates $r\leftrightarrow100/r$) gives a value of $a$, and $a(r)+a(-r)=40$. The ten divisors in $[-10,10]$ form $5$ opposite pairs, so the sum is $5\cdot 40=200$.

**Answer: 200**

arml-2007-team-09.title: Describe the graph of $f$
arml-2007-team-09.body:
For a fixed integer $n\ge1$ and $x\in[n,n+\tfrac1n)$: $f(x)=n\left|x-n-\tfrac1{2n}\right|=\left|nx-n^2-\tfrac12\right|$. This is a "V": $f(n)=\tfrac12$, $f(n+\tfrac1{2n})=0$, and it climbs back to $\tfrac12$ (not attained) as $x\to n+\tfrac1n$.

For larger $x$ in $[n,n+1)$ the rule $f(x)=f(x-\tfrac1n)$ repeats the pattern with period $\tfrac1n$. So on $[n,n+1)$ the graph of $f$ is exactly $n$ copies of this V (each of width $\tfrac1n$, value from $\tfrac12$ down to $0$ and back toward $\tfrac12$).

**Counting intersections.** $g(x)=2^{x-2007}$ is positive and increasing, and $g(2006)=\tfrac12$. The graph of $f$ has values in $[0,\tfrac12]$, so intersections can only occur for $x\le 2006$ (for $x\ge1$ and $g(x)>0$). On each V, the increasing curve $g$ (which lies between $0$ and $\tfrac12$ there) meets the V exactly twice: once on the descending arm and once on the ascending arm. This holds for each V in the region $1\le x\le 2006$ (at $x=2006$ the endpoint value $\tfrac12$ is the top of a V).

The number of V's in $[n,n+1)$ is $n$, for $n=1,\dots,2005$, giving $2(1+2+\cdots+2005)=2005\cdot2006=4{,}022{,}030$ intersections in $1\le x<2006$.

Finally, at $x=2006$ we have $f(2006)=2006\cdot\left|0-\tfrac1{4012}\right|=\tfrac12=g(2006)$, one more common point (the left end of the next V). For $x>2006$, $g>\tfrac12\ge f$, so there are no more. The total is $4{,}022{,}030+1=4{,}022{,}031$.

(The printed key lists $4{,}022{,}030$, which omits the point $(2006,\tfrac12)$.)

**Answer: 4022031**

arml-2007-team-10.title: Count intersections
arml-2007-team-10.body:
There are $\binom n2$ segments, hence $\binom n2$ bisectors. Two bisectors normally meet in one point, giving $P=\binom{\binom n2}{2}$ pairs. The exception: the three bisectors of the sides of a triangle meet in its circumcenter, so each triangle's circumcenter is counted $3$ times (3 pairs) but is only one point. When no four points are concyclic and no two bisectors are parallel, all those coincidences are exactly the $\binom n3$ triangles, so
$$M=\binom{\binom n2}{2}-2\binom n3=\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)(3n-5)}{24}.$$
(This is the maximum since any extra coincidence only decreases the count.)

**Divisibility.** $2007=9\cdot223$. Since $3n-5$ is never divisible by $3$ and exactly one of $n,n-1,n-2$ is, the factor $3$ in $24$ cancels it; so $9\mid M$ requires $27\mid n(n-1)(n-2)$, i.e. $n\equiv0,1,2\pmod{27}$.

For $223\mid M$: $n\equiv0,1,2\pmod{223}$ or $3n\equiv5\pmod{223}$, i.e. $n\equiv76\pmod{223}$.

Searching smallest $n$: $n=223q+r$ with $r\in\{0,1,2,76\}$ and $n\equiv0,1,2\pmod{27}$. The values below $299$ are $2,\dots$ (none work), and $299=223+76$ satisfies $299=27\cdot11+2\equiv2\pmod{27}$.

**Answer: 299**
